section.title: Make Haste to Help Me
section.sectionRationale: A brief, urgent cry for immediate rescue, this psalm is nearly identical to the closing verses of Psalm 40, reused here as its own short prayer 'to bring remembrance,' teaching that God's people may return again and again to the same honest, urgent plea, 'make haste, O God, to deliver me,' without needing new words for every fresh crisis.
section.thesis: David's brief, urgent cry, 'hurry, O Lord, to help me,' models unashamed dependence and urgency in prayer, content to be 'poor and needy' before a God who does not delay, a pattern of honest, immediate appeal that anticipates every believer's confident access to God through Christ.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the urgent cry for God's help against those who seek his harm, verses 1-3; and the wish for the joy of those who love God's salvation and the honest confession of his own poverty and need, verses 4-5.

units.label: Make haste, O God, to deliver me
units.note: the urgent cry against those who seek his harm

verses.text: Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O Lord, to help me!
May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and {{kalam|humiliated}}.
May those who say, "Aha, aha!" retreat because of their shame.

units.label: I am poor and needy
units.note: joy for those who love God's salvation, honest confession of need

verses.text: May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, "Let God be magnified!"
But I am {{ani|poor}} and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O Lord, do not delay.

kalam.gloss: To humiliate, dishonor, or put to shame. David prays this specifically on those who mock and seek his harm, asking that their scheming against him be publicly reversed and exposed rather than succeed.

ani.gloss: Poor, afflicted, needy, often describing someone who has no resources of their own and depends entirely on another. David applies this word to himself even as reigning king, an honest confession of complete dependence on God rather than on his own position or strength.

basic.context: This short psalm is almost identical to the closing verses of Psalm 40, reused here as its own brief, urgent prayer. David cries out for immediate help against those who mock and seek his harm, and closes by honestly naming himself poor and needy before God.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm shows that urgent, repeated prayer is not a lack of faith; David reuses nearly the same words from an earlier psalm, teaching that believers do not need fresh, original language for every new crisis, only honest, urgent dependence on God.
basic.originalLanguages: David prays that his mockers be kalam, humiliated, exposed and reversed in their scheming. And he confesses himself ani, poor and needy, even as reigning king, an honest admission of complete dependence on God rather than his own resources.
basic.typology: David's honest confession, 'I am poor and needy,' even while king, anticipates Christ, who though rich, for our sake became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, taking on the very posture of complete dependence and need that this psalm confesses.
basic.christ: Christ embodies this psalm's posture perfectly, though the eternal Son and rightful King, He emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, becoming poor for our sake so that, in Him, we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9, the ultimate fulfillment of the psalm's honest confession of need.
basic.god: God is shown as one who is called to hurry, to act without delay for those who are truly poor and needy, sovereign over the shame and reversal of those who scheme against His people, and worthy of being magnified by all who love His salvation.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 40:13-17 supplies the nearly identical source text this psalm reuses as its own urgent prayer. 2 Corinthians 8:9 applies the language of voluntary poverty to Christ's incarnation for our sake. Philippians 4:6 echoes this psalm's pattern of urgent, honest prayer brought directly to God without delay.
basic.oneStory: David's honest, urgent cry as one who is poor and needy, repeated nearly word for word from an earlier psalm, anticipates Christ, who became poor for our sake so that all who are truly needy before God might find in Him a help that does not delay.

context.literary:
The psalm is five verses long and built like a hinge. Verses 1 to 3 face outward and downward, at the enemies and at the trouble pressing in. Verses 4 and 5 turn to face God and the company of those who seek Him, and the two halves are held together by a single repeated urgency. The opening is a double imperative, 'Make haste... Hurry,' and the closing is its mirror, 'hurry to me... do not delay.' Everything between is enclosed by that plea for speed, so the whole psalm reads as one breath.

Within the frame the psalm sets two groups against each other by the same verbs. Those who seek my life are to be ashamed and confounded, verse 2, while those who seek You are to rejoice and be glad, verse 4. The word 'seek' is the pivot: the same activity, looking for something, ends in disgrace or in joy depending on the object. The mockers say 'Aha, aha!' in verse 3 and the lovers of salvation say 'Let God be magnified!' in verse 4. One group gloats over a man, the other magnifies God, and the psalm asks that each cry be answered in kind.

The last verse brings a change of voice that the first verses have been preparing for. The 'me' of verses 1 to 3 was a man being hunted. In verse 5 he says who he is, 'poor and needy,' and only then repeats the request for haste. The order matters. He does not claim merit, rank or innocence as the ground of his plea; the only credential offered is need, and the only reason given for hurry is that God is the help and deliverer.

The psalm is also unusually plain in form. It has no narrative, no memory of past rescue and no vow of thanksgiving, which sets it apart from most laments in the Psalter. It is petition in its purest and shortest shape, which fits the superscription's note that the psalm is a prayer 'to bring to remembrance,' a cry meant to be said quickly and to be remembered before God.
context.historical:
The near-identity with Psalm 40:13 to 17 is the fact that shapes everything else. Psalm 40 is a long psalm that opens with waiting patiently, a new song and a delivered life, then turns in its last section to renewed trouble, 'evils without number surround me,' Psalm 40:12. Its closing petition is the passage Psalm 70 lifts out. The Psalter therefore preserves the same five lines twice, once as the end of a longer meditation and once as a prayer standing alone. The compilers evidently thought the lines worth having in both places.

Psalm 70 also carries the marks of the collection in which it now sits. Psalms 42 to 83 are often called the Elohistic Psalter because the divine name 'God' is used far more often there than the covenant name. Psalm 70 shows the process at work. In verse 1 it asks God to deliver and then names the Lord, where Psalm 40:13 asks the LORD twice. In verse 4 the wish is 'Let God be magnified,' where Psalm 40:16 has 'The LORD be magnified.' Whoever placed the psalm here has adjusted the divine name to match its surroundings, which tells us the psalm was handled as living liturgy, edited for use, rather than fixed as a museum piece.

The superscription attributes it to David and calls it a prayer to bring to remembrance. The same phrase heads Psalm 38, another cry of a suffering man. Scholars differ on whether the phrase points to a memorial offering, to the worshiper calling God to remember him, or to a psalm used to remind the congregation. We can be sure of the practical setting the psalm implies: a man in immediate danger, with people jeering at his trouble. The cry 'Aha, aha!' was the sound of a bystander gloating, and it appears in Psalm 35:21 and 35:25 and, aimed at the fallen sanctuary and land, in Ezekiel 25:3. To Israel it was the voice of mockery over someone else's ruin.

The context inside the book matters too. Psalm 69 just before it is a long, desperate lament of a man sinking in deep waters, and Psalm 71 after it is the prayer of a man growing old. Psalm 70 sits between them as a short flare of prayer, the sort of thing anyone in the middle of those longer troubles could say in a single breath.
context.canonical:
Psalm 70 is a hinge in the canon between Psalm 40 and Psalm 71. Psalm 71:12 quotes it closely, 'Be not far from me, O God. Hurry, O my God, to help me,' so the next psalm treats Psalm 70 as an established prayer and builds on it. The chain of prayers shows a Psalter that is not a pile of separate songs but a conversation in which one psalm answers, borrows from and extends another.

The urgent word 'hurry,' chushah in Hebrew, runs through several of David's laments: Psalm 22:19, Psalm 38:22, Psalm 40:13, Psalm 71:12 and Psalm 141:1. It is the vocabulary of a believer who does not think haste is irreverent. Proverbs 1:16 speaks of the wicked whose feet rush to shed blood. Godly haste is the haste of the needy toward their Helper.

The plea 'do not delay' returns at a national scale in Daniel 9:19, where Daniel ends a long prayer of confession with, 'For Your sake, O my God, do not delay.' The prayer of the individual poor man and the prayer of an exiled people share the same last cry. The book of Revelation gives it its final answer, and the church's last word in Scripture is the same urgent invocation, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' Revelation 22:20, answering 'Yes, I am coming soon,' Revelation 22:20.

The theme of the poor and needy runs across the Psalter and the prophets. God listens to the needy, Psalm 69:33, and does not despise His people, and Psalm 72, only two psalms further on, describes the ideal king as the one who will deliver the needy who cry out. Psalm 70 gives the voice of that needy man, and Psalm 72 gives the king who answers him.

The New Testament takes the pattern rather than the words. Jesus teaches His disciples to pray without giving up and promises that God will give justice to His elect who cry out to Him day and night, and that He will do so 'quickly,' Luke 18:7-8. Paul says to bring every request to God, Philippians 4:6. Both stand on the ground the Psalter has prepared, that short, urgent, honest prayers are the kind God answers.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm's authors wanted worshipers to have a prayer that could be said in the worst hour of a bad day, in almost no time, with nothing left over. A longer psalm asks the worshiper to remember, reflect and then request. This one drops the reflection and keeps only the request. That is a deliberate choice about what prayer is for: God is to be asked for help before the person has finished working out what is wrong.

The psalm also means to teach where to place oneself in prayer. The man does not say he is strong, or clever, or on the right side, although in his own eyes he is. He says he is poor and needy, and he lets that be the whole of his standing. This is what the compilers wanted a later reader to grasp: in the sanctuary the honest beggar is the person in the right posture. He is not disqualified by need, he is qualified by it.

A third intention is corporate. By asking that all who seek God rejoice and that those who love His salvation keep saying 'Let God be magnified,' verse 4, the psalm places one man's private emergency inside the life of a whole people. His deliverance is not only for himself. Its purpose is that others will have reason to praise. The psalm is short, but it does not permit prayer to shrink into a private complaint.

The last thing the first hearers were meant to notice is the tension between haste and trust. The man asks God to hurry, and yet the request itself is an act of trust. He believes God can and will act, and that lateness is the only danger. The pair of urgent commands and quiet confidence is what the psalm is built to train.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's actual situation: people are hunting him, jeering at him, and he prays that they will be put to shame. It does not command believers to hate their enemies or to celebrate their downfall, and the imprecation in verses 2 and 3 should be read as a request that God set right what is wrong, not as permission for personal vengeance. Elsewhere Scripture is clear that we are to leave vengeance to God, Romans 12:19, and to pray for those who persecute us, Matthew 5:44. Read with those texts beside it, the psalm asks God to do justice; it does not appoint us to do it.

What the psalm prescribes is a pattern of speech. Ask directly. Ask quickly. Confess need without disguising it. Let the request rise to praise, as verse 4 does. The wish that God be magnified also guards the prayer against self-interest. The man wants help, but he wants that help to end in God's honor.

There is one more caution. The psalm asks for speed, but it does not promise it. The saints in Scripture often wait long for an answer, and some die without seeing it, Hebrews 11:39. The urgency of the prayer is legitimate, but the outcome belongs to God's timing. That is why the same psalm can end with 'do not delay' and still be heard by a God who sometimes seems to delay.

debates.question: Why does this psalm sit in the Psalter as an almost exact copy of the end of Psalm 40?

views.label: Deliberate extraction for liturgical use
views.case: The superscription 'to bring to remembrance' and the changes in the divine name, which suit the Elohistic collection, suggest editors took a portion of Psalm 40 and shaped it as a standalone prayer for urgent occasions.

views.label: Independent use of a shared prayer
views.case: David may have prayed the same words more than once, and both psalms preserve one common prayer. The small variations in verses 1, 4 and 5 fit a prayer used repeatedly in different circumstances.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is right, Scripture itself models reuse. Believers need not feel that a prayer must be new to be sincere, and a well-loved prayer said again in a new crisis is as fitting as a fresh one.

debates.question: How should we read the prayer that enemies be ashamed and turned back?

views.label: A legitimate prayer for God's justice
views.case: The request is addressed to God, not carried out by David, and it asks for shame, not death. The psalms regularly ask God to vindicate the righteous, and Paul quotes such psalms in the New Testament, for example Romans 11:9-10.

views.label: A prayer the New Testament transforms into prayer for enemies
views.case: Jesus commands love and prayer for enemies, Matthew 5:44, and prays for those crucifying Him, Luke 23:34, which suggests that after Christ the right prayer is that enemies be turned back from their opposition, ashamed of it in repentance, rather than destroyed.

debates.bearing: The two readings are compatible. The psalm can be prayed as a request for God to end wickedness, with the hope, learned from Christ, that ending it may include turning the wicked to repentance.

study.originalLanguages:
The cry for haste uses two different verbs across the first verse, and the second, chushah, is the psalmist's own word for urgency. It is an imperative of chush, to hurry or make haste, and it appears in a family of David's laments: Psalm 22:19, Psalm 38:22, Psalm 40:13 and Psalm 71:12. It does not describe a mild wish. The picture is of a person running, and the prayer asks God to run.

Verse 2 pairs two words for shame, bosh and chapher. The first is the ordinary word for disappointment and disgrace, used of those whose hopes collapse. The second means to be abashed or to blush. Together they make a wish for public reversal: those who hunted the man are to find that their plans have been set against them. The verse then says that those who wish him harm should be 'repelled,' turned back to where they came from.

Verse 3 has a pun that English hides. The mockers are to 'retreat because of their shame,' and the Hebrew for 'because of' is eqev, literally 'on the heel of.' The word shares its root with the word for heel, the one from Genesis 3:15. The picture is of shame following at the mockers' heels as they turn and run. It is a small piece of poetic justice: those who stood over a fallen man saying 'Aha' are to find that shame pursues them as they leave.

The word 'Aha,' he'ach, is an interjection of malicious delight. It carries the tone of someone gloating over a rival's fall, as in Psalm 35:21 and Psalm 35:25, and in Ezekiel 25:3 and 26:2 where nations gloat over Israel's ruin. The doubling, 'Aha, aha,' is the sound of a crowd enjoying the spectacle.

Verse 4 uses two verbs for joy together, rejoice and be glad, and describes God's people as 'lovers of Your salvation.' The word for 'be magnified' is from gadal, to grow great, and here it means that God should be made great in the eyes of others. The wish is not that God become greater, which is impossible, but that His greatness be recognised.

The closing verse pairs ani, poor, with evyon, needy. The pair is a stock phrase in the Psalter: it appears here and in Psalm 40:17, and in Psalm 72:12 and 72:13, where the king delivers the needy and takes pity on the poor. Then two nouns, ezer and pelet, help and deliverer, name what God is to the man. The final imperative, al te'acher, 'do not delay,' is the same phrase Daniel uses at the end of his great prayer in Daniel 9:19.

typology.type: The needy man who is helped, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: The man who says 'I am poor and needy' becomes a pattern for the many poor who look to God in the Psalms. In Christ the pattern reaches its fullest sense: He is the One who 'became poor' for us, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and who announces good news to the poor, Luke 4:18. Where David's poverty was a condition he was rescued from, Christ took poverty on freely and made others rich. The correspondence breaks in one place. David was needy because of circumstances and sometimes sin; Christ was needy by choice and without sin.

The gloating of the crowd against the righteous sufferer finds its sharpest form at the cross. Passers-by 'hurled insults' at Jesus, shaking their heads, and the chief priests mocked Him, Matthew 27:39-43. The cry that David asked God to turn back on his mockers was raised over the Son of God. The pattern is fulfilled and inverted: the mockers were not put to shame that day, but on the third day the One they mocked was raised, and every knee will bow before Him, Philippians 2:10-11. The type falls short in that David's deliverance was temporary, while Christ's resurrection is final.

typology.type: The prayer 'Let God be magnified', verse 4
typology.fulfillment: The wish that God be made great in the eyes of many is answered in Christ, through whom, Paul says, God has given the name above every name so that every tongue confesses Jesus Christ is Lord, 'to the glory of God the Father,' Philippians 2:11. David wanted the rescue of one man to lead others to praise; the rescue of Christ leads all nations to praise. The correspondence is real but the scale is transformed, from a single deliverance to the reconciliation of the world.

study.christ:
Psalm 70 leads to Christ by the figure of the needy man. Nothing in it names a king or a Messiah, and it would be forced to make every line a prophecy. But its heart is a confession of need before God, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the One who took that place with full seriousness. Paul writes that though He was rich, yet for our sake He became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and that He emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7. Nothing in Him was pretended. In Gethsemane He asked the Father for help in the hour of His trouble, and in the wilderness He lived by every word from God's mouth, Matthew 4:4.

The psalm is also linked to Christ by the mockers. The 'Aha, aha!' of verse 3 belongs to the family of Psalms 22 and 35, and the New Testament draws on that family repeatedly to describe the cross. The crowd that wagged its head and called out to the dying Jesus, 'He trusts in God; let God rescue Him,' Matthew 27:43, was speaking the voice of Psalm 22:8. The evangelists understood the passion in the light of the laments, and Psalm 70 belongs to the same shelf. If it is a prayer the righteous sufferer prayed, then Jesus is the one who prayed it most truly.

A third link is Hebrews 10:5 to 10, which quotes Psalm 40:6 to 8, the same psalm from which Psalm 70 was taken, and places those words on the lips of Christ: 'Here I am, I have come to do Your will.' Psalm 70 is the petition that came at the end of that psalm. This does not mean Psalm 70 is directly messianic. It means the psalm has a home in a composition the New Testament reads through Christ, and its closing plea belongs to that same voice. The obedience of the Son and the cry of the needy man come from the same person.

The psalm also points to Christ as the answer to its own request. The man asks for a Helper who will not delay. Christ is the Helper God sent 'when the set time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4, and He is described as the One who is able to help those who are being tempted, Hebrews 2:18, because He suffered when tempted. He now sits at the right hand of God and 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near, Hebrews 7:25. The one who prays 'do not delay' has a priest who is already praying with him.

A final guard is needed. The psalm is not a hidden prophecy of the details of Jesus' life. It becomes Christological by pattern, by theme and by the way the whole Psalter is read in the light of Christ, as He Himself said that everything written about Him in the Psalms had to be fulfilled, Luke 24:44.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 70 is a God who can be spoken to in a hurry. The man does not soften his request or pad it with reflections. He says 'hurry,' and 'do not delay,' and he says it to God's face. Behind that is a picture of God that is relational rather than remote. He is the Helper and Deliverer of those who are in need, not a sovereign who must be approached with polished speeches. This is worth noticing because it corrects a common fear, that God resents rough or brief prayer. The Psalter puts these words in the mouth of a king.

He is also a God who takes sides with the needy. The man puts nothing forward but his poverty and his desire for God. God's response to need is the running theme of the Psalter: He 'listens to the needy,' Psalm 69:33, He raises the poor from the dust, Psalm 113:7, and He takes up their cause. The prayer assumes that it is in God's character to answer need with help, and that this is not an exception but the rule.

The psalm shows God as the One before whom enemies are put to shame. It does not say that God does this out of malice, but as an act of justice. The mockers who say 'Aha' are wrong about the God who watches them, and God's action against them is the vindication of His people and His own name. That is why verse 4 ends with 'Let God be magnified.' Deliverance is not a private favor. It makes God visible.

The psalm also touches the doctrine of God's names. In verses 1, 4 and 5 it uses names that differ from those in Psalm 40, shifting toward 'God' in the Elohistic collection. This shows that in Israel's worship the different names were not separate deities but ways of addressing the one God, at once the Creator and the covenant Lord. The same God is 'Lord' who helps the individual and 'God' who is to be magnified among the nations.

The psalm holds together God's greatness and His nearness. He is to be magnified, and yet He is asked to hurry to the side of one poor man. Power and attentiveness do not compete in Him. The One who fills heaven bends to a man who is poor and needy, and He is not made smaller by doing so.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to bring brief, honest cries into the middle of an ordinary day, and to end them with a wish that God be seen for who He is. It also teaches us to allow others their own reasons to rejoice in Him, since the last thing the man asks for is not his own comfort but the joy of everyone who seeks God.

crossReferences.note: The source of this psalm. Psalm 40 ends with a sudden turn from praise to trouble, 'evils without number surround me,' and then the five lines Psalm 70 reuses. Reading the two together shows that the cry for help can come straight after thanksgiving; a believer who has been delivered once still needs to ask again.

The next psalm quotes this one, 'Be not far from me, O God. Hurry, O my God, to help me.' The borrowing shows the Psalter treating Psalm 70 as a prayer people already knew, and Psalm 71 places the same urgency in the mouth of an old man whose strength is failing.

The taunt 'Aha, aha!' appears here in the mouths of false witnesses who gape at David. Psalm 35:25 and 26 then pray, as Psalm 70 does, that the gloaters be ashamed and confounded. The link shows that the cry of Psalm 70:3 is a settled type of mockery in David's prayers.

Another psalm headed 'to bring to remembrance,' Psalm 38 ends with the same urgent imperative, 'Come quickly to help me.' It helps explain the superscription of Psalm 70: this is the kind of prayer a suffering man sends up to be remembered.

Daniel's long prayer of confession ends with 'do not delay.' The same words that David used for a personal emergency are used for the restoration of a whole people, and the pattern shows that God's servants may press for speed, on the ground of His own name.

The psalm before this one ends with 'You who seek God, let your hearts be revived,' because the LORD listens to the needy. Psalm 70:4 and 5 take up the seekers and the needy from the same language. The two psalms seem placed side by side to belong together.

Paul says that though Christ was rich, yet for our sake He became poor, so that through His poverty we might become rich. It is the New Testament's fullest reading of the 'poor and needy' theme: the King took the place of the needy so that the needy could share His riches.

Paul tells believers to let their requests be made known to God by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving. Psalm 70 shows the practice in miniature: it brings the need to God without qualification, and it moves at once from petition to a wish that God be magnified.

Jesus asks whether God will not give justice to His elect who cry out to Him day and night, and promises He will do so quickly. The passage explains how urgent prayer and patient trust fit together: God does hurry, and yet the elect are asked to keep crying out.

The writer urges believers to approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. The 'help' God gives in a time of need answers the plea of Psalm 70:5, 'You are my help,' with a High Priest who has been tempted as we are.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 70 looks small beside the great turning points of Scripture, but it carries one of the Bible's steadiest threads: God's people are always, at bottom, poor and needy. From the beginning that need was part of the human condition. Adam and Eve were given a garden and a task and could not sustain themselves without God's word, and after the fall the need became desperate. Israel in Egypt cried out under its burdens and 'God heard their groaning,' Exodus 2:23-24. The cry of the helpless is the first thing the story of redemption hears.

The story that follows is a series of such cries. The judges period repeats the pattern, Israel in trouble, Israel crying out, God raising up a deliverer. David is the shepherd king who has learned to pray this way, and the Psalter collects his prayers, including this one, as models for later generations. Even a king with an army needs a Helper, and he says so. The psalms then hand those prayers to ordinary people so that a shepherd or a widow in a crisis has words to pray.

The psalm also points to the way the whole story is resolved. The word 'help' has a long life across Scripture, and it finally names a Person. The angel tells Joseph to call the child Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins, Matthew 1:21. The man who prays 'hurry to me, O God' gets his answer in the incarnation and the cross, in which God came to the place of the poor and needy Himself. The gospel is not that the needy learn to stop needing. It is that the Rich One became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and that those who admit their poverty are the ones He fills.

The story also shows how the answer is held back and given at once. The saints of Hebrews 11 saw God's promises from afar and did not receive them, Hebrews 11:13, and the church still prays 'how long.' The delay is real in history, and yet the psalm's confidence is not misplaced, because the Son's resurrection is the first installment of everything the prayer asks for. God has already acted.

In the new creation the need that drives this psalm is finished. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and the poor will no longer be poor. The last prayer of the Bible is the same urgent word in another language, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' Revelation 22:20, and it is answered by the One who says, 'Yes, I am coming soon.' The pattern that begins with a needy man crying 'do not delay' ends in a city where God Himself wipes away every tear and no one has to ask twice.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to do without delay, in verse 1?

options.text: Deliver him and hurry to help him.
options.note: The psalm opens with an urgent double request for immediate rescue.

options.text: Wait patiently until circumstances improve on their own.
options.note: The psalm's request is the opposite, urgent and immediate help, not patient waiting.

options.text: Give him wealth and status.
options.note: The request is for rescue and help, not material gain.

options.text: Send him a sign before acting.
options.note: David asks directly for action, not merely a preliminary sign.

quiz.q: What does David wish for those who love God's salvation, in verse 4?

options.text: That they would rejoice and be glad, saying 'Let God be magnified!'
options.note: This wish contrasts sharply with David's prayer against those who mock and seek his harm.

options.text: That they would remain silent and withdrawn.
options.note: The verse specifically wishes joy and vocal praise, not silence.

options.text: That they would gain political power over others.
options.note: The wish given is joy and praise of God, not political gain.

options.text: That they would receive material riches.
options.note: The specific wish is joy and the exclamation of God's magnification, not material wealth.

quiz.q: How does David describe himself in verse 5, even though he is king?

options.text: Poor and needy.
options.note: This honest confession of complete dependence on God stands even from a reigning king.

options.text: Wealthy and self-sufficient.
options.note: David explicitly names himself poor and needy, the opposite of self-sufficiency.

options.text: Powerful and unshakeable.
options.note: The confession given is one of need and dependence, not unshakeable power.

options.text: Wise beyond all his counselors.
options.note: The specific self-description is poverty and need, not superior wisdom.

quiz.q: This psalm is nearly identical to which other passage in the Psalter?

options.text: The closing verses of Psalm 40.
options.note: Psalm 70 reuses Psalm 40:13-17 nearly word for word as its own short, urgent prayer.

options.text: The opening verses of Psalm 1.
options.note: Psalm 70's parallel passage is the ending of Psalm 40, not the opening of Psalm 1.

options.text: The middle section of Psalm 119.
options.note: The parallel text is specifically Psalm 40:13-17, not any part of Psalm 119.

options.text: The entirety of Psalm 23.
options.note: The near-identical parallel is Psalm 40's closing verses, not Psalm 23.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply this psalm's honest confession of poverty and need to Christ?

options.text: Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake so that we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9.
options.note: This directly parallels the psalm's posture of voluntary, self-emptying dependence and need.

options.text: The New Testament teaches Christ was never in need of anything at any point.
options.note: 2 Corinthians 8:9 and Philippians 2:7 both describe Christ taking on real, voluntary poverty and the form of a servant.

options.text: The New Testament has no connection between poverty and Christ's mission.
options.note: 2 Corinthians 8:9 explicitly connects Christ's becoming poor to the believer's spiritual enrichment.

options.text: Christ's poverty in the New Testament refers only to His lack of physical possessions.
options.note: The New Testament's language in 2 Corinthians 8:9 and Philippians 2:7 refers to Christ's whole self-emptying incarnation, not merely material possessions.

questions: David prays urgently, 'make haste... hurry,' without hesitation or embarrassment. Is there an urgent need in your life right now that you have been hesitant to bring honestly and immediately to God?

This psalm reuses, nearly word for word, an earlier psalm's closing prayer. What familiar prayer, whether from Scripture or your own past, could you return to honestly today rather than searching for new words?
David wishes joy specifically for 'those who love Your salvation,' verse 4. What would it look like for your own love of God's salvation to translate into visible joy today?

David confesses himself 'poor and needy' even as reigning king, verse 5. Where are you tempted to hide your own neediness behind competence, position, or achievement rather than confessing it honestly to God?
Christ became poor so that, in Him, we might become rich. How does reflecting on Christ's voluntary poverty for your sake change how you view your own present need or lack?

translationNotes.note: This psalm closely parallels Psalm 40:13-17, evidence that it was deliberately reused, likely for congregational or personal use as a short, urgent prayer, 'to bring remembrance,' per its superscription.
Humiliated renders kalam, a public reversal of shame, praying that the schemes of those seeking harm would themselves be exposed and turned back.
Poor and needy renders ani, describing someone with no resources of their own; David applies this humbling term to himself even while reigning as king.
